Three studies assessed the accuracy of ultrasound-guided SIJ injections in cadaver models, with conflicting results. In a study by Klauser et al., the accuracy of upper-level and lower-level ultrasound-guided SIJ injections was confirmed using CT. In a total of 20 joint injections, the authors observed IA needle placement at the upper level in 70% vs 90% at the lower level. The overall success rate for ultrasound-guided IA needle placement was 80% (16 of 20 SIJs). Another cadaver study by Perry et al. assessed the accuracy of ultrasound-guided SIJ injections through the dissection of injected paint markers. Out of 17 SIJ injections, 15 (88.2%) were injected in the IA space, but five (33.3%) also showed partial EA spread on ultrasound during initial injection, necessitating redirection of the needle. Three of the 15 IA joint injections exhibited partial EA spread not observed during ultrasound-guided needle placement. Finally, as above, a study by Stelzer et al. compared the accuracy of ultrasound-guided SIJ injections to fluoroscopically-guided SIJ injections, evaluating joint spread by dissection after injection of colored latex. With ultrasound-guided SIJ injections, the IA spread was observed in 5% of injections, with 95% of injections being EA. In contrast, the fluoroscopy-guided SIJ injections showed IA spread in 50%, 40% showed intra-ligamentous spread, and 10% resulted in intravascular uptake. CT-guided sacroiliac joint injections Randomized trial A single RCT compared clinical outcomes with low-dose CT-guided IA SIJ injections to fluoroscopically-guided IA SIJ injections. In a study by Bessar et al., 52 patients with SIJ complex pain were randomized to either low-dose CT-guided IA SIJ injection or fluoroscopically-guided IA SIJ injection and followed for 12 months. In both groups, significant improvements in pain and function were observed through 12 months, with results generally being more favorable in the CT group. In this study, blinding was not reported. Difficulty in localization of the SIJ space was reported in five patients who underwent fluoroscopically-guided injections. More patients were satisfied in the CT group, with no significant difference in the radiation dose between groups. Non-randomized studies Two prospective studies assessed the accuracy and clinical outcomes of CT-guided IA SIJ injections. In a study by Artner et al., 30 patients with LBP and positive SIJ provocation testing underwent low-dose CT-guided bilateral IA SIJ injections, with 100% of injections being IA. The authors also found no significant difference in radiation dose when compared to fluoroscopically-guided IA SIJ injections performed the previous month (4.57 mGycm with low dose CT-guided injections vs 3.73 mGycm with pulsed fluoroscopically-guided injections). The authors did not delineate how accuracy was determined. When the accuracy was assessed using confirmation by a blinded evaluator in a later study by Althoff et al., CT-guided SIJ injections were observed to be IA in 76% of procedures. Three studies retrospectively assessed the accuracy of CT-guided injections. In a study by Bronsard et al., 94 patients with SIJ complex pain after previous lumbosacral spinal fusion surgery underwent up to three CT-guided IA SIJ injections confirmed with arthrography. Out of 146 SIJ injections, 61 were IA, and 41% were effective (>70% pain improvement) two days after injection. It should be noted that patients received repeat injections only if prior injections were ineffective (up to three injections), and the third injection was performed with 3-dimensional surgical navigation. In retrospective studies by Paik et al. and Oren et al., combined CT-guidance with fluoroscopy was used, with both studies reporting 100% IA spread confirmed by arthrography. In the study by Paik et al., the authors found that the time required for combined CT-fluoroscopy procedures was greater than the reported times for fluoroscopically-guided IA SIJ injections, but less than for standard CT-guided, ultrasound-guided, and MRI-guided IA SIJ injections. Q7. Which is more effective for the treatment of sacroiliac joint complex pain, intra- or extra-articular sacroiliac joint complex injections? The SIJ complex is a sophisticated structure composed of the sacral and iliac bones, which form the joint space enclosed by a fibrous capsule and synovial lining. This complex is supported by an extensive network of posterior and anterior ligaments, as well as a diverse group of muscles that contribute to its stability and function. These muscles include the erector spinae, multifidus, gluteal group, psoas, quadratus lumborum, piriformis, obliques, hamstrings, and pelvic floor muscles. The intricate interplay of these osseous, articular, ligamentous, and muscular components ensures the structural integrity and proper biomechanical function of the SIJ complex. Nociceptors are abundantly present throughout these structures, and researchers have used pain provocation techniques and anesthetic studies on both patients and healthy volunteers to develop comprehensive pain referral maps for IA and EA SIJ complex pain. , , , , The probability of EA or IA sources being the primary SIJ complex pain generator depends on many factors. Extra-articular pathology is more likely to be predominant in a young individual with unilateral pain who reports a specific inciting event, and injections into the dorsal ligaments typically require a higher volume than for IA injections. Extra-articular SIJ pain is often associated with exquisite tenderness, and normal or near-normal imaging, although certain MRI sequences such as short tau inversion recovery (STIR) can detect acute inflammatory processes. In contrast, IA pathology is more likely to occur insidiously in an older person with bilateral pain, and is generally associated with radiological abnormalities. Some patients also have IA and EA pathology occurring simultaneously, as suggested by controlled trials demonstrating efficacy for EA injections in patients with spondyloarthropathies, and a trend toward a higher responder rate and greater pain relief when a combination of IA and EA spread was observed (60%) compared to when only IA (48%) or EA (54%) spread occurred ( P = .25) in injection-based outcome studies. In a retrospective study conducted in 120 patients, Borowsky and Fagen reported a higher proportion of responders following combination IA/EA injections than for IA injections alone. In a recent randomized trial by Tantawy and Nazim in which the same dose and volume of corticosteroid and local anesthetic was injected either into or both into (IA) and outside (EA) the joint, the authors found no difference in pain scores at 1 week, but superiority for the combination group at 1- and 6-months (see ). Indirect comparisons from randomized trials There are three placebo-controlled trials that have evaluated outcomes following SIJ injections. In the first one by Maugars et al., 10 patients (13 joints) with spondyloarthropathy and active sacroiliitis were randomized to receive IA corticosteroids or saline following joint arthrography in a double-blind fashion. At 1-month follow-up, five of the six joints injected with corticosteroid were deemed to have ≥50% pain relief vs one of seven in the saline group. At 1 month, six of the seven control joints were reinjected with corticosteroid. At 3- and 6-month follow-ups, 62% and 58% of participants continued to report pain reduction, respectively. In the two randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled trials by the same group of investigators that evaluated EA injections, the authors compared depo-corticosteroid and local anesthetic injections to saline and local anesthetic injections in 20 patients with seronegative spondyloarthropathy in their initial study, and in 24 patients without spondyloarthropathy in a follow-up study. At both 1- and 2-month follow-up, the treatment group experienced a greater reduction in pain than the control group. In addition to the short follow-up periods, another flaw in these two studies is that the local anesthetic used in both treatment groups is not a true placebo. Non-randomized comparative-effectiveness studies In the first study to compare IA to EA SIJ injections, Murakami et al. performed a non-randomized, evaluator-blinded, prospective study in 50 patients comparing immediate-term (5-min post-injection) outcomes for lidocaine IA injections and EA injections performed in four locations along the SIJ. The EA injections were performed with 0.5-1 mL aliquots of lidocaine in areas where hypertonic saline provoked pain. The authors reported significant improvement in six activities of daily living in 100% of the EA injections vs 36% of the IA injections. They then performed EA injections on the IA non-responders, again reporting a 100% response rate. In addition to the unrealistic 100% response rate, other flaws include selection bias and the outcome measure, which was immediate and did not involve pain relief. In an observational study by the same group, the authors performed EA injections in 85 patients with pain around the posterior superior iliac spine. The injectate consisted of 0.5 mL aliquots of 2% lidocaine mixed with contrast in individuals whose pain was reproduced by needle irritation. In those who failed to experience a positive outcome, defined as ≥70% pain relief 15- to 30-min post-injection, a fluoroscopically-guided IA injection was performed with a 50:50 mixture containing betamethasone and bupivacaine 0.5%. Seventy-two (85%) patients experienced a positive response, with the successful group comprised of 81% ( n = 58) EA and 19% ( n = 14) IA injections. Is there an optimal technique for performing intra-articular sacroiliac joint injections and sacral lateral branch blocks? Anatomical considerations When determining the optimal technique for performing IA and EA SIJ injections as well as SLBBs, it is important to consider the anatomy relevant to each procedure. The SIJ, a combination diarthrodial and amphiarthrodial joint, typically consists of the sacral segments S1 (largest component), S2, S3, and the ilium. The SIJ consists of both IA and EA portions. The IA and EA portions consist of a synovial joint (infero-anteriorly) and syndesmosis (ie, fibrous linkage), respectively. The synovial portion of the SIJ typically involves the inferior half of the joint with the articular cartilage on the sacral side being thicker in comparison to that of the iliac side (∼3-5mm vs ∼1-2 mm). Multiple ligaments support the SIJ including ventral, dorsal, transverse and interosseous ligaments. The interosseous ligaments are also supported by the short and long dorsal sacroiliac ligaments. , The volume of the joint has been estimated to range from 0.5-2.5 mL. , , , , The innervation to the SIJ and surrounding structures (posterior EA elements) is complex, and our understanding continues to evolve. , , , The IA portion of the SIJ is mainly innervated by anterior sources with a small contribution from posterior sources. Both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers exist within the articulation of the SIJ. , The anterior aspect of the joint is innervated by branches from the lumbosacral trunk, as well as direct branches from the anterior ramus of L4 and the anterior ramus of L5. Dissection and histology has not confirmed innervation from the anterior rami of S1-S3 and sacral plexus. , The posterior aspect of the SIJ capsule and posterior EA ligaments are innervated by the posterior sacral network (PSN), which predominantly consists of lateral branches of the posterior rami from S1 to S3. demonstrates the location of the posterior interosseous ligaments and sacral lateral branches. The L4, L5, and S4 lateral branches inconsistently innervate the posterior SIJ complex. One study demonstrated contributions from S1 and S2 in 100%, S3 in 88%, L5 in 8% and S4 in 4% of specimens, though other studies have reported greater contributions from L5 and S4. , , , , The lateral branches are small with mean diameters <1 mm (range 0.21-1.51 mm). When the L5 lateral branch is involved in the innervation it may anastomose with the lateral branch of S1 or innervate the posterior aspect of the joint directly. , The lateral branches emerge from the foramina, with the number of lateral branches from each foramen ranging from one to four and most levels having one to two. , Defining optimal technique of each injection procedure depends on its purpose (diagnostic, prognostic, and/or therapeutic) and the relevant structures to be targeted. The following text will focus on diagnostic and/or therapeutic IA SIJ injection and diagnostic/prognostic SLBBs. Optimal technique for therapeutic dorsal ligament complex injection will not be discussed, as its therapeutic value has not yet been well defined (addressed in other sections of this article). Similarly, diagnostic injections of the innervation of the anterior aspect of the SIJ complex will not be discussed here, as viable technique(s) have yet to be validated. Intra-articular sacroiliac joint injections Multiple techniques have been described for IA SIJ injections. For all IA SIJ injections, image guidance is mandatory to assist with accurate needle placement, prevent deposition of the diagnostic and/or therapeutic injectate into vasculature, and to determine if there is IA and/or EA spread. Placement without image guidance results in a high technical failure rate ranging from 78%-100%. Although ultrasound guidance can be used for placement, the use of this imaging modality may be associated with lower accuracy rates in some contexts and long learning curves for IA placement. , , , Therefore, this section will focus on fluoroscopy-guided injections. For fluoroscopy-guided injections, multiple technical aspects need to be considered including the location of SIJ access, use of contrast medium, and volume of therapeutic and/or therapeutic injectate. First, injection of contrast medium is recommended to delineate the eventual spread of the diagnostic and/or therapeutic injectate and to assist with target specificity. Contrast injection allows for the determination of intravascular spread, EA spread into and onto surrounding structures and the existence of ventral and dorsal capsule tears. SIJ contrast flow patterns may have predictive value for short-term outcomes, although their utility for long-term prognosis appears limited. Scholten et al. conducted a retrospective review of 54 subjects who underwent therapeutic SIJ corticosteroid injections, with 49 patients included in the final analysis. Their findings revealed that arthrographic contrast patterns demonstrating injectate delivery to the superior portion of the SIJ were associated with greater pain reduction at 2 weeks post-injection. However, this differential effect was not observed at the 8-week follow-up when compared to subjects whose contrast did not reach the superior portion of the SIJ. A second variable to consider when performing IA SIJ injections is the volume of injectate. When performing SIJ injections into the inferior portion of the joint, the capacity is <2.7 mL with capsular distention occurring at volumes ≤1.6 mL. , , Therefore, it is recommended that volume of injections be <2.5 mL including the volume of contrast deposited prior to any diagnostic and/or therapeutic injectate. This is addressed in additional detail within Question 5 (What volume should be used for SIJ injections? Should diagnostic injections include corticosteroid?) of this article. Traditionally, IA SIJ injections are performed by accessing the lower portion of the joint since the synovial portion of the SIJ involves the inferior half of the joint. However, successfully entering the joint at times can be challenging. Successfully gaining IA SIJ access may be more difficult in male patients. Injections may also be more difficult in individuals who demonstrate osteophytes and the presence of substantial vacuum phenomena on preprocedural CT scans. In general, review of pre-procedural axial imaging may provide insight regarding the most feasible angle of approach for obtaining access to the SIJ. In individuals for whom access is challenging (eg, obesity or severe joint narrowing), the use of CT-guidance may improve technical success and possibly outcomes. If entering the lower portion of the joint is challenging with fluoroscopy and alternatives are not available, other points of access in the middle and superior portions of the SIJ have been suggested. , , In an observational study of 69 consecutive patients in whom the middle portion of 100 separate SIJs was targeted, the success rate was 80%. Notably, in three of the 20 cases of failed SIJ access using the middle part of the SIJ, the traditional inferior SIJ access technique was successful. Conversely, in four patients, attempts to access the inferior aspect of the joint were unsuccessful, with successful injections achieved by accessing the middle portion of the joint. This suggests the need for adaptability. Sacral lateral branch blocks SLBBs are used to select patients for RFA techniques that target the posterior sacral network (PSN) associated with EA SIJ complex pain including the short posterior sacroiliac ligament (SPSL), long posterior sacroiliac ligament (LPSL), interosseous sacroiliac ligament (ISL), and superficial lamina of the sacrotuberous ligament (STL). Both single-site, single-depth SLBBs and multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs have been examined for their ability to effectively anesthetize the posterior SIJ complex. , In a randomized, controlled, double-blinded study, single-site, single depth SLBBs were found to be physiologically ineffective on a consistent basis with 60% of volunteers in the active group maintaining sensation with both repeated SIJ capsular distention as well as probing of the dorsal ligaments of the SIJ complex. Furthermore, in a parallel anatomic study examining S1 and S2 lateral branch injections with green dye, only 36% of lateral branches were successfully captured using the single-site, single-depth technique. Based on this study, it was determined that single-site, single-depth SLBBs are associated with a high false-negative rate and may fail to identify patients with pain arising from portions of the posterior SIJ complex innervated by the PSN. In a follow-up, double-blind, placebo-controlled study performed in 20 asymptomatic volunteers, multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs produced a much lower false-negative rate in comparison to the single-site, single-depth SLBBs. For the multi-site, multi-depth SLBB technique described by Dreyfuss et al., needles were placed 8-10 mm lateral to the posterior sacral foramina at multiple locations based on clock face positions around the S1 and S2 foramina (Right: 2:30, 4:00, and 5:30; Left: 9:30, 8:00, and 6:30) and S3 foramina (Right: 2:30, 4:00; Left: 9:30 and 8:00). After ruling out vascular needle tip position with injection of contrast medium at each target area, 0.2 mL of local anesthetic was injected. A second injection at each target area was then performed after withdrawing the needle by one bevel length, for a total volume of 1.2 mL at the S1 and S2 foramina, and 0.8 at S3. When using this multi-site, multi-depth SLBB protocol, 70% of the active group did not respond to posterior ligamentous probing after receiving injections compared to 0-10% of the sham group. Furthermore, a parallel cadaver study revealed a 91% accuracy rate for multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs to capture the S1 to S3 lateral branch nerves. Notably, in the human subject portion of the study, 86% of participants retained the ability to sense capsular distention; thus, the ventral articular portion of the SIJ is not effectively anesthetized by blocking the PSN. One study has validated an ultrasound-guided technique for SLBBs using the Dreyfuss et al. multi-site, multi-depth SLBB protocol. In this randomized-controlled trial, the investigators probed the dorsal aspect of the sacroiliac ligament, the dorsal aspect of the SIJ, and the SIJ interosseous ligament both before and after implementing two different SLBB protocols in order to establish the ability of participants to perceive pain in these regions and then to evaluate the degree to which pain to probing was reduced or completely eliminated by each of the two SLBB protocols. The investigators reported a similar degree of ability to block nociception caused by probing these three SIJ complex structures when using the previously validated fluoroscopically-guided multi-site, multi-depth SLBB protocol compared to their ultrasound-guided “triple injection” technique. This technique consisted of injecting 0.5 mL of 2% lidocaine at target points along the sacral lateral crest lateral to the S1 foramen, between the S1 and S2 foramina, and between the S2 and S3 foramina. In conclusion, fluoroscopically-guided multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs (using the Dreyfuss et al. protocol) effectively target posterior EA SIJ structures with lower false-negative rates than single-site, single-depth SLBBs. In addition, ultrasound-guided multisite blocks along the sacral lateral crest (according to the Finlayson et al. protocol) effectively target posterior EA SIJ structures to a comparable degree according to one randomized controlled trial. Therefore, if one is contemplating an RFA procedure to interrupt the PSN, multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs or ultrasound-guided multisite blocks along the

lateral crest lateral to the S1 foramen, between the S1 and S2 foramina, and between the S2 and S3 foramina. In conclusion, fluoroscopically-guided multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs (using the Dreyfuss et al. protocol) effectively target posterior EA SIJ structures with lower false-negative rates than single-site, single-depth SLBBs. In addition, ultrasound-guided multisite blocks along the sacral lateral crest (according to the Finlayson et al. protocol) effectively target posterior EA SIJ structures to a comparable degree according to one randomized controlled trial. Therefore, if one is contemplating an RFA procedure to interrupt the PSN, multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs or ultrasound-guided multisite blocks along the sacral lateral crest (according to the Finlayson et al. protocol) should be favored as a prognostic tool. However, it should be noted that sham-controlled studies that did not to use prognostic SLBBs have yielded positive RFA outcomes, , while controlled studies that used SLBBs have yielded negative or equivocal results. In addition, if a patient has relief with an IA SIJ injection, it may not predict the ability of an RFA technique that targets the PSN to effectively mitigate pain since these RFA techniques do not target IA sources of pain as demonstrated in the study by Dreyfuss et al. Summary: When performing IA SIJ injections, the preferred method includes fluoroscopic guidance, access to the inferior (synovial) portion of the SIJ, use of contrast medium to confirm appropriate spread of subsequent diagnostic and/or therapeutic injectate (if no allergy/contraindication), and a low injectate volume (<2.5 mL); Grade B recommendation, moderate level of certainty. If IA access is not possible using the inferior aspect of the joint, consideration can be given to accessing the middle or superior aspects of the joint or, if available, using CT guidance; Grade C recommendation, low-to-moderate level of certainty. When considering radiofrequency ablation (RFA) to interrupt the sacral lateral branch nerves (posterior sacral network) for treating posterior sacroiliac joint complex pain, fluoroscopic guidance should be used to perform multi-site, multi-depth sacral lateral branch blocks (SLBBs) targeting the lateral branches of S1 through S3; Grade C-B recommendation, moderate level of certainty. Ultrasound-guided multisite blocks along the sacral lateral crest (according to the Finlayson et al. protocol) targets posterior extra-articular SIJ structures and may be considered for prognostic SLBBs; Grade C recommendation, low level of certainty. Q9. Should sedation be used for intra-articular sacroiliac joint injections? Should sedation be used for sacral lateral branch blocks? Should sedation be used for sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation? The use of sedation for interventional pain procedures is controversial. The debate arises secondary to whether providing analgesic/anxiolytic medications can alter the patient’s “true” response to the intervention. Accurate or “true” responses from the patient are critical to render a diagnosis or predict (prognosticate) outcome for diagnostic injections. In the context of this article, “sedation” will be referred to as the provision of a sedative and/or analgesic medication (eg, benzodiazepine and/or opioid, respectively) as opposed to the patient’s physiologic response. The use of sedation during interventional pain procedures is not uncommon. The use of sedation has been found to vary depending on the procedure being performed. A survey study by Kohan et al. found that sedation was used in 80% of RFA procedures, 66% of sympathetic nerve blocks, 54% of epidural corticosteroid injections, 50% of medial branch nerve blocks, and 42% of the time for SIJ injections. Benzodiazepines and opioids were the most commonly used sedatives. An international survey study found that only 29% of physicians “never” use sedation for SIJ injections. Whereas the use of sedation can help decrease patient-related discomfort, decrease patient movement, possibly improve patient satisfaction, decrease the incidence of vasovagal reactions, , and possibly decrease the risk of false-negative responses, it may increase the risk of false-positives responses, thereby negatively impacting the diagnostic and/or prognostic nature of the procedure. , Improved patient satisfaction with the use of sedation has not been firmly established. Kubulus et al. found improved patient satisfaction with the use of sedation during regional anesthetic injections; however, this study was limited by its retrospective nature and confounding anxiety that may have been experienced secondary to the surgical procedure. Other studies report conflicting results. Cucuzella et al. found that 17% of patients requested intravenous diazepam prior to an initial epidural corticosteroid injection, with 28% requesting it again for subsequent procedures. Higher pain scores, increased anxiety, and depression were associated with requests for repeat sedation, which may explain the paradoxical observation that the use of sedation was associated with increased procedure-related pain. A follow-up study by the same group of authors found that even after an extensive discussion regarding sedation, 58% of patients chose either anxiolysis (oral diazepam) or sedation (IV diazepam) prior to an injection and 93% of those who chose to receive no anxiolysis or sedation were satisfied with their decision. Similar to Cucuzella et al. who reported higher pain scores in sedated patients, the authors reported lower satisfaction scores in patients who received sedation, though this observation may represent selection bias (ie, patients with increased anxiety and pain sensitivity may be more likely to elect to receive sedation) and the small number of patients who received sedation prevented a meaningful statistical comparison. Analgesia from opioids may decrease pain, making it difficult for the clinician to determine if post-procedural pain relief was related to opioid administration or the intervention itself. Benzodiazepines cause skeletal muscle relaxation and thus may decrease back pain in patients with a myofascial component. Additionally, benzodiazepines and opioids may alleviate the affective (anxiety) component of pain and alter post-procedural activity, thereby undermining the accuracy of the post-procedural analgesic response. Effect of sedation during diagnostic or prognostic procedures on treatment outcomes: Indirect evidence Several studies have evaluated the effect sedation during prognostic blocks has on neurolytic or RFA outcomes, albeit none for sacral lateral branch RFA. Although a small retrospective study found poorer neurolysis outcomes when sedation was used during prognostic celiac plexus blocks, a larger study ( n = 265) evaluating the effect of sedation during genicular nerve blocks on RFA results reported no effect on treatment outcomes. , A randomized trial evaluating methoxyflurane on pain during and after genicular nerve blocks reported rapid recovery for the short-acting inhaled medication used worldwide for out-of-hospital posttraumatic analgesia. The authors recommended consideration of its use for other prognostic procedures based on the tenet that a block’s predictive value will be higher when the local anesthetic effect outlasts the duration of sedation. Guidelines Societies, including the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) and the International Pain and Spine Intervention Society (IPSIS), recommend against the routine use of sedation for most interventional pain procedures except for advanced procedures (vertebral augmentation, spinal cord stimulation, etc.). Studies report an increased risk of overall complications and serious neurological injuries with the use of moderate or heavy sedation. A recently proposed local coverage determination (LCD) asserts that the use of moderate or deep sedation, general anesthesia, or monitored anesthesia care (MAC) is not indicated for SIJ injections and is not considered medically reasonable or necessary. The LCD does note that use of anxiolytics may be indicated in patients with anxiety disorders and needle phobias. Additionally, the LCD panel noted that sedation not only increases risk but may also compromise the validity of the diagnostic procedure. Diagnostic sacroiliac joint injections Direct Evidence Cohen et al. examined the impact of sedation with midazolam and fentanyl on the diagnostic validity of SIJ injections and sympathetic blocks in a randomized, controlled crossover trial. The use of sedation was found to result in lower pain diary scores and a higher proportion of positive diagnostic injections than for injections performed without sedation, suggesting a possible increase in false-positive injections. Although procedure-related pain scores were lower in injections performed with sedation, sedation did not improve patient satisfaction or 1-month treatment outcomes. Therapeutic sacroiliac joint injections Direct evidence No studies were identified. Indirect evidence: sedation for pain-relieving procedures Dreyfuss et al. found no difference in post procedure pain scores assessed immediately after a therapeutic epidural corticosteroid injection without local anesthetic between patients who had received sedation with midazolam and/or fentanyl and those who did not. Sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation Although the use of sedation is rarely indicated with SIJ injections, it can be indicated during SLBRFA according to the subject matter expert (SME) panel in the recent LCD. In addition to multiple lesions at multiple levels, “finder” needles (if used) are often placed in 3-4 sacral foramina as landmarks for electrode placement, and can elicit radicular pain. How effective are non-invasive treatments for sacroiliac joint complex pain? Non-operative (conservative) treatments for sacroiliac joint pain Non-operative or conservative management of SIJ complex pain commonly includes a trial of analgesic and anti-inflammatory medications, physical therapy (PT) modalities, bracing, psychological therapies, acupuncture, and various other treatments. Although supported by little evidence, these treatments are frequently recommended before consideration of operative or procedural treatments. Despite the lack of medium or high-quality evidence, conservative treatments are recommended for the treatment of SIJ complex pain by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and commercial payors in the United States. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services require 4 weeks of conservative care prior to performing procedures on the SIJ complex. There is disagreement among professional guidelines, with some expert medical consensus recommending conservative care based on low-quality evidence , and others recommending against a requirement due to the lack of moderate or strong evidence of efficacy. Many clinical studies evaluating IA SIJ injections, SLBRFA, and SIJ fusion have required a course of conservative treatment, , , , , while others have not. , The rationale behind the de facto use of conservative management of SIJ complex pain is primarily based on the presumption that SIJ complex pain, like many musculoskeletal conditions, will improve on its own with time, and low-risk conservative measures may facilitate this. However, the typical clinical course of SIJ complex pain in the absence of formal treatment has not been reported in the literature. The rationale for a mandatory trial with conservative therapy may be a more reasonable assumption for acute than chronic SIJ complex pain in which symptoms have persisted despite time and self-care, and conservative treatments can pose a financial burden. In an RCT by Cohen et al., the control group who received a cluster of conservative measures had a poor response rate, with only 11% having a positive outcome with three months of therapy. It must also be acknowledged that the majority of studies evaluating the effectiveness of various non-invasive treatments for sacroiliac joint complex pain did not use SIJ injections and/or SLBBs to confirm the diagnosis of SIJ complex pain. As such, a proportion of the individuals in these studies likely did not have SIJ pain given the known limitations of history, physical examination, and imaging for identifying a painful SIJ complex. What is the evidence for non-corticosteroid injections in the treatment of sacroiliac joint complex pain? Corticosteroids are the most used injectable treatment for SIJ complex pain. Whereas corticosteroid injections are an effective treatment for SIJ complex pain, relief may be short-lived for some individuals. , , Unwanted systemic and local side effects of corticosteroid use are well described. , As such, physicians and scientists have proposed alternative treatments to overcome the relative limitations of corticosteroid use. Numerous other potentially therapeutic injectable agents have been proposed, including autologous orthobiologics, allogeneic orthobiologics, hyaluronic acid, prolotherapy, chemoneurolysis, botulinum toxin, and saline. These proposed therapeutic agents can be classified according to the tissue being targeted for injection (articular, ligamentous, and neuronal). Regenerative agents may contain properties that promote repair of dense fibrous tissues such as joint capsules, ligaments, and fascia. These injectates fall into one of two categories: (1) naturally occurring bioactive agents [eg, platelet rich plasma (PRP)] and/or extracellular structural components (eg, hyaluronic acid); and (2) irritating or debriding solutions that initiate endogenous repair mechanisms (eg, prolotherapy, saline). IA injections are theorized to relieve pain through mitigation or reversal of degenerative changes to the articular cartilage of the SIJ. Literature reports of IA injectates that have been investigated as potential treatments for SIJ complex pain include autologous and allogenic orthobiologics (specifically platelet-rich plasma, platelet-rich fibrin, Wharton’s jelly placental allograft ; and hyaluronic acid , ). Dextrose-based prolotherapy and saline injections into and surrounding the SIJ have also been reported. Whereas vigorous lavage with saline may provide a “washout” of inflammatory and pain-mediating molecules from the interior joint space, this is unlikely to occur with a single IA injection; however, introduction of fluid within the joint may indirectly stimulate an anti-inflammatory cascade if proteoglycans are removed from the superficial extracellular matrix of articular cartilage. The rationale for EA injection of regenerative agents into structures of the posterior SIJ complex is to relieve pain by strengthening or “tightening” damaged or lax ligaments in order to improve stability. Hypertonic dextrose prolotherapy purportedly induces cell proliferation at ligamentous attachment sites. There is also an existing report of EA injection of PRP into the posterior SIJ complex. The second class of therapeutic injectates target neural tissues with the goal of relieving pain by interrupting or altering nociceptive signal transmission from the SIJ complex. Published literature includes two types of injectable therapies to potentially treat SIJ complex pain: Phenol-based chemoneurolysis and botulinum toxin A. Phenol is a non-specific protein coagulant; aqueous solutions have previously been injected in both the IA and EA spaces for the purpose of neuronal coagulation. Currently, there is only one publication describing the use of botulinum toxin, which was injected into the EA structures of the posterior SIJ complex. Although best known as a paralytic agent that interferes with synaptic signaling at the neuromuscular junction, there is evidence that botulinum toxin A acts on sensory neurons as well. , Proposed mechanisms include reduction of neurogenic inflammation, alterations of efferent and afferent signals in spinal nerves leading to decreased central sensitization and inhibition of the release of sensory neuropeptides, as well as inhibiting protein translocation from the endosomal compartment to the cell plasma membrane of transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and Transient Receptor Potential Ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) receptors. Herein, we describe the published evidence related to effectiveness within each category of potentially therapeutic injectable agents. Notably, no sham-controlled (explanatory) RCTs were identified addressing the efficacy of any non-steroid injectables to treat pain specifically arising from the SIJ complex. What is the evidence for cryoablation in the treatment of sacroiliac joint complex pain? Cryoablation of peripheral nerves leads to cellular destruction and temporary or permanent interruption of pain signal transmission along the affected nerve pathway by applying extreme cold to the target nerve, causing ice crystal formation within the nerve cells and surrounding tissue. Cryoablation may cause less extensive damage to surrounding tissues and may allow for better preservation of the nerve’s connective tissue structures (endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium) compared to RFA. This relative preservation of the nerve’s scaffold can potentially facilitate remyelination and nerve regeneration in some cases, depending on the intensity and duration of the freezing process. Other benefits of cryoablation may include: Creation of large volume lesions, less procedural pain, and lower cost compared to some RFA technologies, though this depend in part on the system used and how costs are attributed. Evidence-base for treatment of sacroiliac joint complex pain The literature search revealed very limited published evidence addressing the clinical outcomes of cryoablation for SIJ complex pain. Two case series and one retrospective study were identified. One case series included five cases in which patients were selected for cryoablation used a diagnostic IA SIJ injection with 3 mL of 2% lidocaine. A strip-lesion technique of cryoablation was used to capture the S1, S2, and S3 lateral branch nerves. The authors reported that patients experienced “more than 50%” pain relief for up to 6 months after SLB-cryoablation using combined ultrasound and fluoroscopic-guidance. Another case series included two patients who were treated with cryoablation (without a prior prognostic injection). The authors did not report which nerves were included (L5 dorsal ramus, sacral lateral branch nerves, or both). The authors reported that both patients experienced 50% pain reduction up to the end of the 4-month follow-up. In a retrospective case-control study, outcomes in 39 patients treated with cryoablation for SIJ complex pain were compared to 44 patients who underwent IA SIJ corticosteroid injection. In the cryoablation group, participants were selected using a single IA SIJ injection with 1% lidocaine that resulted in ≥50% pain reduction. Both groups demonstrated statistically significant pain relief at 1-, 3-, and 6-months compared to their baseline pain scores. However, the cryoablation group demonstrated a larger magnitude of pain relief and a greater proportion of responders based on using both a ≥ 50% pain reduction and complete pain relief thresholds as the definitions of “treatment success”. Extrapolation of evidence for treatment of similar conditions A randomized, placebo-controlled, single-blind study compared RFA, cryoablation and sham cryoablation in 120 patients who reported >50% pain relief following high-volume (2 mL) peri-articular lumbar facet injections. Ablations were performed with small radiofrequency electrodes (22-gauge) and large cryoablation (14-gauge) probes. The authors reported no difference between groups with regard to any outcome measure except for improvement on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale in the cryoablation group, but not the RFA group at 6 months post-procedure. In a narrative review evaluating cryoneurolysis for knee osteoarthritis, non-specific knee pain and post-arthroplasty knee pain (14 studies, 3 RCTs), Diep et al. found evidence for improvements in pain, quality of life, function and opioid consumption. However, the low quality of the trials (10 targeted only the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve, while 4 did not report the neural targets) led the authors to the conclusion that while promising, cryoablation for knee pain remains investigational. Summary: There is insufficient evidence to assess the efficacy and effectiveness of cryoablation for SIJ complex pain; Grade I evidence. Recommendation: Further studies, including RCTs, are warranted. Future studies should include investigation of anatomically valid techniques for sacral lateral branch nerve capture, like what has been done in clinical trials and other outcome studies evaluating SLBRFA. Q13. Is sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation effective for the treatment of sacroiliac joint complex pain? SLBRFA is the process of coagulating the neural tissues of the posterior sacral network (PSN), which is comprised of sensory fibers from the L5 dorsal ramus and sacral lateral branches of the S1-S4 dorsal rami, in order to disrupt nociceptive signals from the EA structures and posterior bony cortex of the posterior SIJ complex. , , Variations of this procedure have been applied for over two decades by interventional pain physicians. In a 2001 retrospective case series, Ferrante et al. first attempted RFA by lesioning the posterior inferior part of the posterior joint by sequentially walking bipolar radiofrequency cannulas cephalad in the joint space as far superior as possible. The authors reported 35% of patients experienced ≥50% pain relief through 6 months. Although these results established the feasibility of RFA, future investigations that targeted the nerves themselves would go on to yield more robust findings as subsequent advances in our understanding of PSN neuroanatomy has led to the development of increasingly comprehensive and anatomically-valid lesioning protocols. Numerous reports have now been published that address the efficacy and effectiveness of SLBRFA. Some of these studies have used anatomically validated techniques for capturing the sacral lateral branch nerves ( ), while others failed to do so. In addressing the question as to whether SLBRFA is effective, it is necessary to specifically evaluate anatomically-valid procedural techniques, as other techniques potentially represent modifications that are not likely to capture the sacral lateral branch nerves and therefore result in predictable technical failure (ie, small-gauge electrodes placed perpendicularly near the foramina, or a single longitudinal electrode placement technique do not provide precision or flexibility for anatomic differences). Here, we catalogue the RCTs within the published literature and describe in detail those that used an anatomically-valid SLBRFA technique. Q14. What nerves should be targeted (dorsal innervation) during sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation? There are several (sometimes contradictory) reports on innervation of the SIJ complex leading to ongoing debate on this topic, with the most inconsistent reports pertaining to the ventral part of the SIJ complex. One of the earliest reports on SIJ complex innervation is from Horwitz, who during the dissection of 114 human cadaveric pelvises, traced numerous branches from the first and second sacral nerves to the long and short posterior sacroiliac ligaments. In a subsequent monograph by Solonen, the author described extensive innervation of the SIJ complex emanating from the S1 and S2 spinal nerves dorsally, and ventrally from L3-S2 spinal nerves. Ikeda reported posterior SIJ complex innervation arising from the L5 and sacral dorsal rami and anterior innervation arising from the L5 and S2 ventral rami. Bradley asserted that the nerves innervating the posterior portion of the SIJ complex are closely associated with the interosseous and sacrotuberous ligaments. The main nerve trunks in this region vary significantly in diameter, with the fifth lumbar nerve descending vertically near the S1 superior articular process, then dividing into lateral and medial branches. The lateral branch joins up with the first sacral nerve, while the medial branch curves beneath the lumbosacral facet joint and enters the multifidus muscle. Bradley described a complex network of nerves, including branches from the fifth lumbar and first to fourth sacral nerves, which contribute to the innervation of the posterior sacral region and sacroiliac ligaments, which was named the “Posterior Sacral Network” (PSN) by Roberts et al. demonstrates the location of the posterior interosseous ligaments and sacral lateral branches. In the 1990s, two studies evaluating the innervation of the SIJ complex were published, one by a Japanese author and the other by German authors. In the earlier study by Ikeda in which 13 specimens (26 SIJ complexes) were examined anteriorly, and 7 specimens (14 SIJ complexes) were examined posteriorly, the authors reported dorsal innervation, which was consistent with earlier findings, but also identified extensive ventral innervation (see ). According to macroscopic examination, the author found the upper ventral portion of the SIJ complex to be innervated by the ventral ramus of the fifth lumbar nerve in seven cadavers bilaterally, and in two unilaterally, for an innervation rate of 61.5%. The lower ventral portion of the joint was supplied by the ventral ramus of S2 or branches from the sacral plexus in eight dissections unilaterally, and in the remaining five dissections bilaterally, for an innervation rate of 69.2%. In the dorsal upper part of the SIJ complex, the lateral branch of the L5 dorsal ramus penetrated the posterior and interosseous ligaments of the SIJ on seven of the 14 hemipelves (50%). Innervation arising from S1 dorsal rami was observed in three hemipelves from three specimens (21.4%). In the lower portion of the dorsal SIJ, 100% of the branches were mainly directed to the SIJ after a network of communication between the S2 and S3 lateral branches, which the authors referred to as the “dorsal plexus.” Additionally, in 21.4% of specimens, SIJ complex innervation was derived directly from the dorsal ramus of S3. In 2002, Vilensky et al. examined histological staining patterns of ligamentous tissue adjacent to the medial aspect of the posterior superior iliac spine and sacrum obtained from six patients scheduled for posterior SIJ arthrodesis. Using the gold chloride staining technique, the authors reported both myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers, as well as mechanoreceptors. However, when they tried to confirm their findings using immunohistochemical staining for protein gene product 9.5, the presence of axons, nerve fascicles, or mechanoreceptors could not be conclusively identified. When immunohistochemical staining for substance P (a neuropeptide associated with pain signaling) was performed, reactive components were identified, but due to background staining, the authors could not definitively conclude these components represented neural tissue. In a 2008 immunohistochemical study by Szadek et al., the authors confirmed the presence of Substance P- and CGRP-immunoreactive fibers in tissue obtained from anterior and posterior interosseous ligaments surrounding the SIJ. During dissection, the authors observed small fibers from the lumbosacral plexus traveling toward the anterior SIJ ligaments. Since RFA treatments for SIJ complex pain target the posterior portion of the joint and associated dorsal ligaments, the most recent anatomical studies have focused on this part of the joint complex. Only one study by Cox et al. focused on the ventral portion of the joint, finding small branches originating from either the L4 ventral ramus (10%), the L5 ventral ramus (80%), or from both the L4 and L5 ventral rami (10%). A study by Roberts et al. further defined the dorsal SIJ complex innervation in order to inform optimal SLBRFA technique. One study found a prevalence of transitional anatomy in 26% in patients with low back pain. Among these patients with low back pain, the prevalence of SIJ complex pain was 28.5% in those with transitional anatomy vs 10.8% in those with normal lumbosacral anatomy, with sacralization of L5 being particularly common. In these individuals, because the SIJ extends more cephalad, there are biomechanical alterations that increase the likelihood of pain, especially when the altered anatomy is unilateral, and theoretically a greater likelihood of L5, or even L4 (which often assumes the innervation pattern of L5), innervating the superior joint. , Summary: The dorsal innervation to the SIJ is complex and variable between individuals, with most high-quality cadaveric studies demonstrating innervation from S1 to S3 in over 90% of specimens. S1 to S3 should be targeted close to the lateral margin of the neural foramina in all patients undergoing SLBRFA; Grade A recommendation, high level of certainty. Given variability between individuals, physicians should consider also targeting the L5 dorsal ramus (in those with transitional anatomy or upper SIJ complex pain) and the S4 lateral branch when the foramen is located at or above the inferior margin of the SIJ, to ensure the most complete posterior SIJ complex denervation possible; Grade B recommendation, moderate level of certainty. Q16. Who are the best candidates for sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation? Identifying the most appropriate patients for any interventional procedure is important. Appropriate selection may be even more critical for procedures involving the SIJ complex due to its intricate anatomy and varied presentations. , Numerous studies demonstrate marked referral map variability in selection criteria when investigating SIJ complex denervation. , , It is likely that different areas of the SIJ complex contribute to these different referral patterns. Thus, given that SLBRFA does not disrupt all the afferent input from the SIJ complex, identifying which referral patterns are most conducive to SLBRFA could improve outcomes and promote economic savings. Approximately 15%-30% of mechanical LBP predominantly below L5 can be attributed to SIJ dysfunction. In addition, identifying the ideal nerves to target and optimizing the cutoff threshold used to delineate a diagnostic or prognostic injection as “positive” have been the focus of investigation. Clinical and psychosocial factors have also been investigated. Failure of non-invasive therapies Treatment options for SIJ complex pain include conservative therapies such as PT, yoga, tai chi, chiropractic care, acupuncture, analgesic medications, as well as minimally-invasive IA, EA injections, SLBB, SLBRFA and SIJ fusion surgery. The noninvasive modalities and joint injections can all be considered first-line therapies under different circumstances and may be offered to the patient based on a shared decision model. A progression of SLBB followed by SLBRFA is typically offered after failure of noninvasive therapies. General factors associated with decreased response to invasive procedures In a multicenter study aiming to identify responders to various LBP procedures, Cohen et al. found that individuals with greater disease burden, depression, sleep dysfunction, concomitant pain conditions, smoking history, and obesity were more likely to fail interventions, indicating a need to address these comorbid conditions prior to or concurrent with procedures. Additional factors reported to be associated with poorer outcomes to invasive procedures include psychosocial pathology (poorly controlled depression or anxiety, poor coping skills, high levels of catastrophizing, untreated substance use disorders, and sedentary life-style), greater disease burden (opioid use, numerous previous failed treatments, higher pre-procedure pain scores, and reduced physical function), central sensitization, and work-related factors (disability, secondary gain, poor job satisfaction, performing manual labor). , Demographic and clinical factors In their bi-institutional study evaluating outcome predictors for SLBRFA, Cohen et al. reported that sex, physical examination signs (including SIJ tenderness, positive Patrick’s test, positive Gaenslen’s test), previous surgery, etiology, concomitant medical conditions, and disability claims, were not predictive of outcome in 77 patients with SIJ complex pain. One consideration for the lack of association between provocation tests and outcomes may be that provocation tests are more likely to reproduce pain from IA vs EA pathology, as most studies examining correlations between exam maneuvers and interventional procedures have used IA injections. Since SLBRFA reduces pain primarily from EA pathology, commonly used “SIJ provocation maneuvers” on physical examination may be less predictive of SLBRFA outcome. Most prior randomized studies have reported favorable results despite requiring one or no provocative tests as a criterion for enrollment. , , Referral patterns and opioid use may also impact outcomes. Although not statistically significant, Cohen et al. noted a higher percentage of unsuccessful outcomes in patients with pain radiation below the knee and on chronic opioid therapy, which is consistent with studies evaluating RFA outcomes for other regions. , , , Since <30% of SIJ complex-associated LBP produces pain distal to the knee and there is a high false-positive rate for diagnostic injections, many of these patients may be misdiagnosed. Baseline opioid consumption has been shown to decrease the likelihood of treatment success in other studies assessing the effectiveness of RFA interventions for chronic LBP as well as other chronic pain conditions. , , Pre-procedure pain intensity, duration of symptoms, and age ≥65 years also increased the odds of failure in the study by Cohen et al. It is not uncommon for duration of symptoms, a hallmark of greater disease burden, to be negatively correlated with outcomes, which can be a consequence of neuroplasticity or refractory psychosocial issues. , In a retrospective study by Amatto et al., the authors also found younger age to be associated with a higher odds for success for SLBRFA. Whereas age has not traditionally been found to be a negative predictor for outcome, it may play a larger role in SLBRFA outcomes given that older patients are more likely to have IA as opposed to EA sources SIJ complex pain. These results suggest that while no single demographic or clinical variable strongly influences outcome, selecting patients without risk factors for treatment failure may improve success rates. Prognostic/diagnostic procedures Number and type of injections The SIJ is complex with numerous potential pain generators. The sacral lateral branches do not run at a consistent depth or location on the sacrum. Therefore, single-site, single-depth SLBBs may fail to consistently anesthetize the nerve supply. The use of multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs may more effectively target the sacral lateral branches. Dreyfuss et al. reported the use of multi-site, multi depth SLBBs resulted in staining of 91% of targeted nerves in cadavers. The authors also reported a 70% clinical success rate, defined as no evoked pain following EA (interosseous and dorsal sacroiliac ligament) and dorsal IA SIJ entry when using this technique. Most patients, however, did report pain upon joint distension. Given these findings, the authors concluded that IA or single-site, single-depth SLBBs may not reliably predict ideal candidates for SLBRFA compared to multi-site, multi-depth SLBBs. Among RCTs, all three studies that used prognostic SLBBs reported positive outcomes at the primary endpoint. , , Dual injections are thought to decrease false-positive rates and increase diagnostic accuracy, though a false-positive rate with dual injections ranging between 12.5% and 26% has been reported. , , Most studies to date have used single injections or IA corticosteroid injections as selection criteria for SLBRFA, possibly leading to inappropriate patient selection. Yet, the few studies that have been performed do not show that more rigorous selection criteria lead to better SLBRFA outcomes. Cohen et al. reported no correlation between a positive SLBB, multiple positive SIJ injections, or percent pain relief (50%-79% vs ≥80%) from diagnostic injection(s) and SLBRFA outcomes. Several other studies also suggest no association between the use of multiple prognostic injections and SLBRFA outcomes. , , In the recent study by Amatto and colleagues, the authors found no differences in outcome stratified by single or double blocks (SIJ or lateral branch), 2 vs 1 SLBB, and 50% vs 80% cutoff thresholds, though in univariate analysis those who experienced <80% pain relief with only a single SLBB fared slightly worse. What is the ideal technique and evidence for performing sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation? Significant variation in the posterior sacral neuroanatomy poses challenges to successful treatment with SLBRFA. There are numerous techniques described for SLBRFA treatment. The largest fluoroscopic anatomical study to date correlated the location of the sacral lateral branches of 40 hemipelves to the published SLBRFA techniques. It found that standard monopolar techniques published at the time of the study did not reliably capture the sacral lateral branch nerves; thus, such techniques are not anatomically valid and should not be used. Several bipolar strip lesion techniques, and one icRFA technique using new targets published in 2018 were considered anatomically valid, achieving expected 100% capture of the lateral branches in 95% or more of the specimens. The Simplicity probe (multi-electrode radiofrequency cannula) technique was not considered anatomically valid, as the described technique can result in the probe being too far from the periosteum where the nerves lie, thus eluding capture. This is consistent with the fact that the only clearly negative sham-controlled trial of SLBRFA used this technology. Sensory stimulation used to guide denervation during radiofrequency treatments has been described in clinical studies. , However, this technique is not described in fluoroscopic anatomical detail, and thus, cannot be validated anatomically. There is clear evidence of lack of sensitivity of electrical stimulation for identification of electrode contact or close proximity to sensorimotor nerves. In the lumbar spine where there is usually one medial branch being targeted; two prospective studies provide conflicting evidence for a correlation between sensory stimulation and lumbar facet RFA outcomes. , For SLBRFA, where multiple nerves carrying sensory information can converge on a single foramen, obtaining concordant sensory stimulation for a single nerve even at low thresholds cannot guarantee interruption of nociception. In animal and ex vivo models, the size and type of RFA probe tip used and the lesioning parameters influence the size and shape of the ablation zone formed, which are critical in determining procedural success. , , To date, however, most ablation zone measurements of RFA techniques have been made using ex vivo chicken breast or bovine liver models. , , Ex vivo study of RFA lesion characteristics is intrinsically limited by lack of blood perfusing through the subject tissue. Chicken breast and bovine liver are homogeneous tissues without adjacent osseous structures, which makes them suboptimal surrogates for predicting in vivo response to SLBRFA. In vivo tissue effects of icRFA and standard monopolar RFA procedures in rats have been studied with MRI prior to sacrifice and verification through histological analysis. Structural changes with icRFA may outlast those lesions created with conventional RFA. This has been shown in retrospective data analyses but has not been formally studied in clinical trials, though one study found that among successful SLBRFA procedures, there was a slower success drop-off rate with icRFA compared to conventional. , A small, in vivo human study of icRFA MRI lesion size showed significant lesion morphology variability at the same targets and between different target locations. Notably, the icRFA coagulation zone volume was significantly smaller at periforaminal sacral locations compared to lumbar medial branch target locations [0.6915 (±1.08) vs. 1.685 (±2.51) cm ] despite using the same size probe tip (4 mm) and lesion parameters. It was determined that icRFA probe placement very close to bone negatively altered the shape and reliability of the ablation zone. Although this study was small, it is known that bone disperses radiofrequency energy, with these results providing a potential explanation for inconsistent results of SLBRFA outcomes associated with icRFA and other RFA techniques. As noted above, icRFA, especially using the targets defined in 2018, and several bipolar strip lesion techniques appear to be the most anatomically-valid SLBRFA techniques, though these findings are based on ex vivo lesion size data, with limited clinical data to confirm or challenge these assumptions. The theoretically increased capture rate, and ensuing improved effectiveness, are particularly important given the anatomical variability in the number and location of sacral lateral branches. Clinical studies use heterogenous selection criteria, which limit comparison of SLBRFA techniques to a degree. Due to several factors including selection and RFA technique heterogeneity, a recent systematic review downgraded the original “high” quality evidence rating to “moderate” quality evidence that SLBRFA provides clinically-significant reductions in pain and disability for up to one year. Q18. What are the most common complications with sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation and how can they be minimized? Potential and reported complications of sacral lateral branch radiofrequency ablation SLBRFA has been shown in numerous studies to improve quality of life in well-selected patients if performed safely and in a technically sound manner. Because it is elective, aggressive prevention of complications is paramount. Adequate data collection regarding complications and research on preventing complications is critical to establishing and maintaining patient and clinician confidence in the safety of this procedure. Data on complications from SLBRFA are usually collected and reported as part of clinical studies. Although common complications are usually self-limiting, rarer but more serious or even catastrophic complications may need to be garnered from sources such as large databases, quality and safety reports (ie, from the Food and Drug Administration) or even from autopsy reports. In theory (never before reported), and based on proximal anatomy, such complications could include rectal perforation or injury to nerves of the sacral plexus innervating the bladder or bowel. In addition to the theoretical potential for injury to the sacral plexus and rectum, SLBRFA may cause predictable complications such as RFA of other peripheral nerves, skin burns, infection, hematomata, localized neuritis, sensory disturbance at the skin due to denervation of cutaneous nerves branching from sacral lateral branches, and a localized increase in persistent pain following thermal lesioning. A systematic review by De Salvatore et al. reported on complications in the analyzed studies that included the largest and most rigorous RCTs performed, finding that the majority related to post-procedure local complications such as increased localized pain, transient paresthesias and hematoma. No serious complications were reported. In some cases, it can be difficult to distinguish from inflammatory post-procedure pain. Specific complications Neuritis and other forms of post-procedural pain As noted above, neuritis is a risk for all ablative procedures and may present as worsening pain of neuropathic quality. In some cases, it can be difficult to distinguish from inflammatory post-procedure pain. In a placebo-controlled trial evaluating icRFA in 28 patients, Cohen et al. reported that a majority of patients experienced temporary worsening of pain lasting between 5 and 10 days attributed to either the procedure itself or temporary neuritis, though only one reported paresthesias. This study did not use preventative corticosteroids or non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs before or after lesioning. In a large, multicenter, randomized trial comparing icRFA to standard medical management that did not report on the procedural use of prophylactic corticosteroids, Cohen et al. reported that 11 of 96 patients experienced worsening pain in the lower back or around the SIJ complex, but the presence of neurological symptoms was not reported. In a small, retrospective study by Hegarty evaluating SLBRFA using a 10-cm single mono- and bipolar electrode in 11 women, two patients reported new paresthesias surrounding the SIJ complex, while a third patient reported a burning sensation 3-months post-procedure that responded to infiltration with local anesthetic and corticosteroid as well as topical lidocaine. The authors recommended post-procedure bupivacaine and corticosteroid as a possible preventive measure to reduce the incidence of neuritis and postprocedural pain. The prevention of neuritis has been evaluated in several studies, most for lumbar medial branch RFA. Although one small, randomized trial found that post-RFA pentoxifylline or corticosteroids reduced the severity of post-procedure pain compared to saline, a larger retrospective study failed to find benefit for post-lesioning corticosteroid injection. In the only study that included patients who underwent SLBRFA with icRFA technology ( n = 2 out of 39 patients and 47 procedures), Fitzpatrick et al. found a 0% incidence of neuritis based on numerical rating scale pain scores and the administration of Douleur Neuropathique 4 Questionnaires (DN4) in both patients who received post-procedure corticosteroids (betamethasone) at ablation sites and those who did not. Although the DN4 score was lower in the non-corticosteroid group (0.1 vs 0.4), both values fell far below the 4-point cutoff required to detect neuropathic pain, and this difference was no longer statistically significant when accounting for repeat procedures. A 2025 systematic review that included two studies not limited to any region concluded that post-RFA corticosteroid administration has not been demonstrated to reduce the risk of post-procedure neuritis. The effectiveness of adjuvants and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to prevent post-RFA neuritis has been reported, also with mixed results. A large retrospective study performed in 215 patients who underwent lumbar and cervical medial branch RFA found a non-significantly lower incidence of neuritis in individuals taking gabapentin for at least 2 weeks prior to the procedure (7.1% vs 13.2%). However, a later retrospective study by Singh et al. conducted in 164 patients found no difference in the incidence of neuritis post-lumbar medial RFA based on whether patients were receiving pre-procedure membrane stabilizers and antidepressants. In a placebo-controlled study performed by Ma et al. in 66 patients, the authors found that 3- and 7-day post-treatment regimens with diclofenac significantly reduced post-procedure pain compared to placebo. Aside from the small, underpowered retrospective study by Fitzpatrick et al., a major limitation in most of these studies was the failure of the investigative team to discriminate between neuritis secondary to nerve ablation and inflammatory post-procedure-related pain from radiofrequency cannula insertion. Impact of radiofrequency ablation on existing implanted devices Monopolar RFA of innervation to the SIJ complex involves the use of electrical current that emerges from the tip of the radiofrequency cannula and flows through the body before exiting through the dispersive electrode (a.k.a., grounding pad). Electromagnetic fields created from the use of short-wave diathermy can result in interference with the functioning of implanted electrical devices (eg, battery and electrical leads) such as deep brain or spinal cord stimulators. A retrospective chart review examining interference of implantable devices following lumbar medial branch, peripheral nerve, and SIJ complex monopolar RFA found no alteration in implantable device function. Although this single study did not discuss the location of the implantable device, the safe use of monopolar lumbar medical branch RFA has also been reported in a patient with deep brain stimulators, with one of the implanted pulse generators located in the anterior abdominal wall. following lumbar medial branch, peripheral nerve, and SIJ complex monopolar RFA found no alteration in implantable device function. Although this single study did not discuss the location of the implantable device, the safe use of monopolar lumbar medical branch RFA has also been reported in a patient with deep brain stimulators, with one of the implanted pulse generators located in the anterior abdominal wall. Similar to lumbar medial branch nerve RFA, a procedure in which the grounding pad is usually placed on the lower extremity, SLBRFA theoretically carries a lower risk in the case of an implantable device placed in the torso or chest as the dispersive pad can be placed at a distance greater than the recommended 15 cm away from the leads and battery. It may, however, present a greater risk of damage to implanted device placed in the low back or below the iliac crest as many spinal cord stimulators are implanted in the gluteal region, meaning the current will likely pass near the implantable device before exiting at the grounding pad. If using monopolar RFA, placing the grounding pad close to and caudal to the RFA site will reduce the size of the induced electromagnetic field. This will minimize the risk of heating the neurostimulator battery and electrodes. However, placing the grounding pad too close to the RFA site can increase the risk of tissue burns, particularly when using high current, long activation times, and the use of conductive fluid, since the energy has less tissue through which to dissipate. There is some evidence that bipolar RFA may be safer than monopolar RFA in patients with implanted devices, with report of its safe use for cervical and lumbar medial branch RFA. In bipolar RFA, the electromagnetic field is limited to the tissue region between the two electrodes, which is significantly smaller compared to the distance between a monopolar RFA electrode and the grounding pad (when the grounding pad is placed at a safe distance away from the RFA electrode side to prevent a skin burn). In a position paper by IPSIS, the authors recommended consultation with the device manufacturer and cardiologist or electrophysiologist, with consideration of the following: (1) Having on-site support for interrogation of the cardiac device during the procedure in the event that reprogramming of the device is required; (2) Placing a magnet over the device to inhibit triggering the device by RFA; and (3) Removing the magnet or using external defibrillator/pacing electrodes in case cardiac arrhythmias occur during the RFA procedure. Radiofrequency ablation in proximity to surgical hardware In the context of lumbosacral or SIJ fusion, the interventionalist may encounter posterior surgical hardware during a SLBRFA procedure. Indeed, SIJ complex pain is more prevalent in patients with arthrodesis of L5 to the sacrum, as the SIJ complex becomes the “adjacent segment” accepting greater forces post-fusion compared to when the L5-S1 segment (or additional lumbar segments) remains mobile. As such, the interventionalist must be aware of safety considerations when SLBRFA is performed in this context, as an RFA electrode may be placed in close proximity to posterior surgical hardware. Cadaveric and human studies have demonstrated that direct contact of an RFA electrode with pedicle screws results in heating , of metal. In a 2015 cadaveric study, investigators observed significant temperature changes in pedicle screws and surrounding soft tissues when an RFA electrode directly contacted a screw, compared to control conditions. The thermal impact was more pronounced with titanium screws than with stainless steel. Specifically, titanium screw heads exhibited temperature increases of 6.66°C, and screw tip temperatures increased by 16.72°C when the RFA electrode was positioned directly over the screws and heated to 80°C for 90 s. Alternatively, stainless steel screw heads demonstrated temperature increases of 4.4°C at the head and 2.46°C at the tip under similar conditions. A 2016 human study evaluated temperature changes at posterior surgical hardware during lumbar medial branch RFA procedures. A temperature probe was inserted via a cannula adjacent to posterior hardware to monitor temperature changes during each RFA procedure. The investigators observed that pedicle screw head temperatures increased in six out of the 10 RFA procedures. Notably, in two cases, temperatures escalated to 42°C, necessitating termination of the procedure. The clinical implications of this depend on hardware location. If hardware is contained completely within corticated bone, it is unlikely that adjacent soft tissues (including neural structures) would be heated. However, in cases of hardware malpositioning (for example, a pedicle screw that breaches the spinal canal), heating of the hardware may be of concern. Separately, in a patient with minimal tissue (either due to intrinsic body habitus or weight-loss following surgery) separating the head of a pedicle screw from the skin, screw heating could cause a skin burn. Notably, this risk remains theoretical (never before reported in the published literature).
